In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the noninvasive assessment by PET of MBF and MFR in DM and obesity is a promising new tool to better understand and monitor diabetic vascular complications.

DM and obesity, in the presence or absence of insulin resistance, have a profound impact on the function of both the coronary microcirculation and the macrocirculation and that PET imaging is a valuable noninvasive tool to assess the pathophysiology and to monitor the effects of therapeutic interventions.
PET imaging of myocardial flow and MFR in patients with DM provides valuable information about the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying diabetic vascular disease and its athero-thrombotic sequel.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the coronary microcirculation plays a key role in the pathophysiology of DM, and that noninvasive assessment with PET is a powerful tool to study the pathophysiology, monitor the response to therapy, and predict outcome in DM.

PET imaging of the coronary microvasculature is a promising noninvasive tool to assess the effects of obesity and DM on vascular function, which is important for patient care and the development of novel therapeutic approaches.

PET imaging of myocardial blood flow and coronary vasodilatation is an invaluable tool for understanding the pathophysiology and monitoring the effects of therapeutic interventions on diabetic vasculopathy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
noninvasive imaging of the coronary microcirculation in DM is feasible, and that it can be used to monitor the response of coronary circulatory function to antidiabetic therapy.
PET imaging can be applied to investigate the pathophysiology of coronary circulatory disorders and to monitor their treatment response in DM.
PET-guided noninvasive evaluation and management of the diabetic coronary circulation has the potential to become a valuable tool for the personalized prevention of diabetic vascular complications.
